Volume 12 · Chapter 09

Time series, forecasting and financial econometrics

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v12-c08, v10-c07

By the endAnalyze persistent and dependent economic series with model-specific inference.

Volume 12 · Chapter 9

Time series, forecasting and financial econometrics

An economic series carries its history into the next observation. Persistence changes forecast uncertainty, an integrated level changes a regression's normalization, and volatility can be stationary while some unconditional moments fail to exist. More observations do not repair an inference formula built for a different probability law. This chapter develops explicit models in which the forecasts, limits and failures can be proved.

Capability. Construct stable causal filters, distinguish recoverable innovations from named economic shocks, derive a stable autoregressive limit and a special unit-root limit, analyze a common trend with a stationary spread, separate GARCH moment regions, and evaluate overlapping forecasts without reusing the evaluation sample as training data. The six worked cases are original synthetic calculations, not evidence about actual asset returns or macroeconomic series.

Prerequisites. Chapter 8 separates identification from estimation and calibration. We also use convergence and statistical targets, least squares, the symmetric spectral theorem, smooth replacement for normal limits, the integrable iid strong law, and Brownian continuity and quadratic variation. No general dependent-data or functional central limit theorem is presumed.

1. Stationarity, causal filters and the information set

A process is strictly stationary if every finite-dimensional distribution is unchanged by a common shift of its time indices. Covariance stationarity requires finite second moments, constant mean and covariance depending only on lag. Strict stationarity alone does not provide those moments. White noise here means a centered, constant-variance, serially uncorrelated sequence; it need not be independent. Conditional-mean forecasts below use the stronger assumption of independent innovations. With merely white noise, the same orthogonality formulas generally describe linear projections.

Let ε_t be iid over all integer dates, with mean zero and variance σ²>0. If ∑ψ_j²<∞, the finite sums ∑_{j=0}^m ψ_jε_{t−j} are Cauchy in mean square: the squared norm of a tail is σ² times the corresponding sum of ψ_j². Completeness gives a limit X_t. Its covariance is γ_k=σ²∑_{j≥0}ψ_jψ_{j+k} for k≥0, with convergence by Cauchy–Schwarz. The process is causal: only present and past innovations enter. For absolutely summable coefficients the series also converges absolutely almost surely, because E∑|ψ_jε_{t−j}|≤E|ε_0|∑|ψ_j|<∞. The common measurable functional of a shifted iid history is strictly stationary.

Write L X_t=X_{t−1}. An ARMA(p,q) relation is Φ(L)X_t=Θ(L)ε_t, with Φ(z)=1−φ₁z−…−φ_pz^p and Θ(z)=1+θ₁z+…+θ_qz^q. Causality concerns a convergent past-shock representation of X. Invertibility concerns recovering ε_t from current and past X. Cancel common polynomial factors before discussing a minimal representation. For example, Θ=Φ permits the solution X=ε even when the uncancelled coefficients suggest persistence.

A sufficient root argument, including repeated factors. Given a factorization of the cancelled denominator into factors (1−az)^m with |a|<1, each inverse has coefficients binom(j+m−1,m−1)a^j. This follows by multiplying m geometric series: the coefficient counts m nonnegative indices summing to j. These coefficients are absolutely summable; a fixed polynomial in j times |a|^j is summable. Finite convolution of absolutely summable sequences is absolutely summable, since the sum of absolute convolution coefficients is at most the product of the absolute sums. Multiplication by the finite numerator preserves this property. Thus this factorization gives a causal L² solution. Its roots z=1/a lie outside the unit circle. Applying the same argument with Φ and Θ interchanged gives a sufficient invertibility condition. This uses ordinary polynomial factorization, not an assertion that failure of a causal condition excludes anticipative stationary solutions using future shocks.

For the explicit ARMA(1,1),

X_t=φX_{t−1}+ε_t+θε_{t−1}, |φ|<1,
ψ₀=1, ψ_j=(φ+θ)φ^{j−1}, j≥1.

Multiplying the geometric inverse (1−φL)⁻¹ by 1+θL proves this formula. Direct covariance summation gives

γ₀=σ²[1+(φ+θ)²/(1−φ²)],
γ₁=σ²[(φ+θ)+(φ+θ)²φ/(1−φ²)],
γ_k=φ^{k−1}γ₁, k≥1.

If |θ|<1, inversion gives ε_t=∑_{j≥0}(−θ)^j(X_{t−j}−φX_{t−j−1}); the series converges in L² by absolute coefficient summability and a uniform L² bound on stationary X. The coefficients of X are 1 at lag zero and −(φ+θ)(−θ)^{j−1} at lag j≥1. With the entire observed past and known parameters, the current innovation is therefore recoverable. A finite observed history requires an initialization treatment; it does not literally supply an infinite past.

Under that information contract, future innovations are independent of current information. Iterating the recursion yields h-step conditional mean φ^hX_t+θφ^{h−1}ε_t for h≥1 and forecast error ∑_{j=0}^{h−1}ψ_jε_{t+h−j}. Its variance is σ²∑_{j=0}^{h−1}ψ_j². Gaussian innovations make this conditional error exactly Gaussian; coefficient estimation uncertainty is absent because the parameters are known. The inspected MIT stationarity and ARMA notes provide the surrounding terminology; these filters and conditions are derived here.

Worked example 1: a forecast and a nonunique shock representation

Take φ=1/2, θ=1/3, σ²=9/4, X_t=2 and recovered ε_t=−3/2. Then ψ_j=(5/6)(1/2)^{j−1} for j≥1, γ₀=13/3 and γ₁=35/12. Forecast means at horizons 1,2,3 are 1/2,1/4,1/8. Error variances are 9/4,61/16,269/64. Their limit as h increases is the stationary variance 13/3; the conditional mean tends to zero.

A separate stationary Gaussian MA(1) with θ=2 and innovation variance 1 has γ₀=5, γ₁=2 and zero covariances after lag one. The invertible representation with θ=1/2 and innovation variance 4 has exactly the same covariances. Both processes are centered Gaussian, so every finite observed vector has the same law. Recoverability and a normalization can select an innovations representation, but observational covariance alone has not identified a physical economic shock.

2. Vector prediction is not structural shock identification

For a VAR(1), let X_t=AX_{t−1}+u_t with iid centered vector innovations, covariance Ω, independent of the prior history. Suppose ||A^j||≤Cr^j for constants C<∞ and r<1 in the Euclidean operator norm. The causal series X_t=∑_{j≥0}A^ju_{t−j} converges in L²: the mean squared tail is bounded by tr(Ω)∑||A^j||². Independence gives

Γ=∑_{j≥0}A^jΩ(A′)^j,
Γ=AΓA′+Ω.

The series is absolutely convergent entrywise and shifting its index proves the Lyapunov equation. If two finite covariance matrices solve it, their difference H satisfies H=A^nH(A′)^n for every n; its norm tends to zero, so H=0. This proves existence and uniqueness under the power bound, without an inconsistent vectorization convention. For a VAR(p), stacking the current and p−1 lagged vectors gives a companion VAR(1). A demonstrated geometric power bound for that companion matrix is a sufficient route to the same result; no unrestricted stability or estimation theorem is being assumed.

Known-parameter forecasts have mean A^hX_t and error covariance V_h=∑_{j=0}^{h−1}A^jΩ(A′)^j. Independent Gaussian innovations give an exact conditional Gaussian distribution. With Gaussian errors, positive-definite Ω held fixed, a full-rank common-regressor sample and conditioning on the initial lagged values, maximizing the conditional likelihood over an unrestricted coefficient matrix yields equation-wise OLS: the derivative of the quadratic residual term is zero at the normal equations. This conditional statement does not discard a parameter-dependent stationary initial-state density from an unconditional likelihood. Its sampling inference requires a separate score limit and variance argument; the scalar result proved below is not a general VAR estimator theorem.

A zero coefficient on another series' lags can encode a predictive exclusion given a specified information set and model. It is not a causal claim about an intervention. If u_t=Bz_t with iid standard Gaussian z_t, then BQ gives the same Ω=BB′ for every orthogonal Q. The entire Gaussian reduced-form law stays the same, while the responses A^hB to named coordinates of z can change. Structural restrictions, institutional evidence or an actual design must select the interpretation. The inspected MIT VAR notes discuss these distinctions; no general LR, bootstrap or impulse-response confidence theorem is imported.

Worked example 2: equal observable laws, different named responses

A=((1/2,1/4),(0,1/3)), Ω=((1,1),(1,2)), X_t=(2,−1)′.

The squared Frobenius norm of A is 61/144<1, so ||A^j||₂≤(√61/12)^j proves the required power bound. Solving the three scalar Lyapunov equations gives Γ₂₂=9/4, Γ₁₂=57/40 and Γ₁₁=479/240. Also A²=((1/4,5/24),(0,1/9)); the two-step forecast mean is (7/24,−1/9)′ and its covariance is ((13/8,4/3),(4/3,20/9)).

Take B=((1,0),(1,1)) and Q=((3/5,−4/5),(4/5,3/5)). Then BQ=((3/5,−4/5),(7/5,−1/5)), and both factors reproduce Ω. The first named shock's impact is (1,1)′ under B but (3/5,7/5)′ under BQ. After one period the responses are (3/4,1/3)′ and (13/20,7/15)′. The predictive model did not change; the unverified structural label did.

3. A complete stable Gaussian autoregression limit

Consider the narrower model X_t=φX_{t−1}+ε_t with a fixed |φ|<1, iid ε_t∼N(0,σ²), σ²>0, and stationary X₀∼N(0,γ₀), γ₀=σ²/(1−φ²), independent of all future innovations. There is no fitted intercept. Put D_T=∑_{t=1}^T X_{t−1}², S_T=∑X_{t−1}ε_t and φ̂−φ=S_T/D_T. Conditioning on the full lagged vector (X₀,…,X_{T−1}) fixes ε₁,…,ε_{T−1}; only ε_T remains random. The conditional score is Gaussian, but its mean is generally ∑_{t<T}X_{t−1}(X_t−φX_{t−1}) and its variance is σ²X_{T−1}². It is not the centered N(0,σ²D_T) law obtained by falsely treating all score innovations as independent of that design.

Denominator and consistency. For jointly centered Gaussian U,V, Cov(U²,V²)=2Cov(U,V)². To verify it when Var(U)=a>0, write V=(c/a)U+η, where η is independent centered Gaussian with variance Var(V)−c²/a; expansion using E[U⁴]=3a² gives the identity. Here γ_k=γ₀φ^{|k|}, so

E[D_T/T]=γ₀,
Var(D_T/T)≤(2γ₀²/T)[1+2∑_{k≥1}|φ|^{2k}]→0.

For s<t, X_{s−1}ε_sX_{t−1} is measurable before ε_t, whose conditional mean is zero. Thus score terms are orthogonal and Var(S_T)=Tγ₀σ². It follows that S_T/T→0 in L² and φ̂→φ in probability. Positivity of γ₀ makes division legitimate with probability tending to one.

From a dependent score to independent quadratic terms. Let Z₀=X₀/√γ₀ and Z_t=ε_t/σ for 1≤t≤T; these are independent standard normals. Expanding X_{t−1}=φ^{t−1}X₀+∑_{j=1}^{t−1}φ^{t−j−1}ε_j gives S_T=Z′K_TZ, where K_T is symmetric with zero diagonal and

K_{0t}=σ√γ₀ φ^{t−1}/2,
K_{jt}=σ²φ^{t−j−1}/2, 1≤j<t≤T.

The absolute sum of row zero is at most σ√γ₀/[2(1−|φ|)]. Every other row is bounded by σ√γ₀/2+σ²/(1−|φ|), using the geometric sums on both sides of its diagonal. Call the larger bound C. Every eigenvalue λ has |λ|≤C: choose a coordinate of an eigenvector with maximal absolute value and apply that row bound to the eigenvalue equation. This bound is uniform in T for the fixed stationary parameters.

The symmetric spectral theorem diagonalizes K_T by an orthogonal matrix. Orthogonal rotation preserves the joint standard-normal density, since it preserves squared Euclidean length and has Jacobian of absolute value one. The rotated coordinates G_j are therefore still independent standard normals. Because tr(K_T)=0,

S_T=∑_{j=0}^T λ_j(G_j²−1),
2∑λ_j²=Tγ₀σ².

The second identity follows either by expanding the Gaussian quadratic form or by its already computed variance. Define a_j=λ_j/√(Tγ₀σ²). Then 2∑a_j²=1 and max|a_j|≤C/√(Tγ₀σ²)→0. Moreover E|G²−1|³≤E(G²+1)³=15+9+3+1=28, so the sum of absolute third moments of a_j(G_j²−1) is at most 14 max|a_j|→0.

The needed triangular-row normal limit, proved. Replace each independent centered term U_j=a_j(G_j²−1) by an independent normal V_j with the same variance 2a_j². For a bounded C³ function f with bounded first three derivatives, third-order Taylor remainder is at most ||f‴||∞|u|³/6. In one replacement the sum of all other terms is independent of U_j and V_j; expected first- and second-order terms cancel. Telescoping bounds the difference in smooth expectations by ||f‴||∞∑(E|U_j|³+E|V_j|³)/6. The first sum tends to zero above. The second is a constant times ∑|a_j|³≤max|a_j|/2 and also tends to zero. The independent normal replacements sum exactly to N(0,1).

For completeness, turn smooth convergence into CDF convergence. Use q(v)=1−35v⁴+84v⁵−70v⁶+20v⁷ on [0,1], extended as one below zero and zero above one. Its first three derivatives match at the endpoints, and q′=−140v³(1−v)³≤0. For fixed δ>0, q((x−z+δ)/δ) and q((x−z)/δ) bound 1{x≤z} below and above. Applying the smooth result gives lower and upper limiting probabilities between Φ(z−δ) and Φ(z+δ). Let δ↓0. This proves S_T/√(Tγ₀σ²)⇒N(0,1), without an unproved dependent-data CLT or characteristic-function continuity theorem.

Combining the score limit and denominator law gives √T(φ̂−φ)⇒N(0,σ²/γ₀)=N(0,1−φ²). The residual variance estimator σ̂²=T⁻¹∑(X_t−φ̂X_{t−1})² equals T⁻¹∑ε_t²−S_T²/(TD_T). The first term tends to σ² by the iid law; the score is O_P(√T), D_T is of order T, and the second term is O_P(1/T). Hence σ̂²→σ² and (φ̂−φ)√D_T/σ̂⇒N(0,1). This is a fully scoped stationary Gaussian result, not a uniform statement as φ approaches one.

4. At a unit root, a different limit appears

Now change the law to X₀=0 and X_t=X_{t−1}+ε_t, with iid N(0,σ²) innovations and no intercept or trend in the fitted regression, using T≥2. For every T the vector of normalized levels X_t/(σ√T), t=0,…,T, has exactly the law of the Brownian grid W(t/T): successive increments are independent centered normals of variance 1/T. This is equality of finite-dimensional laws, not an appeal to a general functional CLT.

On a common Brownian path, continuity gives the Riemann-sum limit D_T/(σ²T²) in law to J=∫₀¹W(s)²ds. More precisely the Brownian-grid version converges almost surely to J. Also telescoping squares gives the exact identity

S_T=∑X_{t−1}ε_t=[X_T²−∑ε_t²]/2.

The Brownian-grid quadratic sum Q_T=∑[W(t/T)−W((t−1)/T)]² has mean 1 and variance 2/T, so Q_T→1 in L². The numerator and denominator therefore converge jointly in probability on that Brownian construction to (W(1)²−1)/2 and J. The latter is positive almost surely: if a continuous path has integral of its square zero it is identically zero, which would force W(1)=0, an event of probability zero.

T(ρ̂−1)⇒[W(1)²−1]/(2J),
(ρ̂−1)√D_T/σ̂⇒[W(1)²−1]/(2√J).

To justify the second expression, use the same exact residual identity σ̂²=T⁻¹∑ε_t²−S_T²/(TD_T). Here S_T is O_P(T), D_T/T² has a positive limit in law, and S_T²/D_T is O_P(1); its contribution after division by T vanishes. Thus σ̂²→σ². The displayed statistic has a Brownian-functional law, not the stable normal reference. Changing initialization, adding deterministic regressors, augmenting lags, using local-to-unity sequences or permitting general innovations requires a new argument. No numerical Dickey–Fuller or residual-cointegration critical values are supplied.

Worked example 3: one stable reference and one unit-root record

For the stationary model φ=1/2, σ²=3/4, γ₀=1 and the limiting variance of √T(φ̂−φ) is 3/4. These quantities come from the stable law, not from a unit-root formula evaluated mechanically at φ=1.

For a separate four-date synthetic unit-root record, let increments be (1,−1,2,1), starting at zero. Levels are (0,1,0,2,3); D_T=5, ∑X_{t−1}X_t=6 and S_T=1. Thus ρ̂=6/5, residual sum of squares is 34/5 and σ̂²=(34/5)/4=17/10. The scaled slope change is T(ρ̂−1)=4/5. The conventional statistic has square 2/17 and value approximately 0.342997170285. The record is an arithmetic illustration; four observations do not verify a Brownian limit or justify normal critical values.

5. A stationary spread can join nonstationary levels

Use a fully specified system: x₀=0, x_t=x_{t−1}+u_t with iid N(0,σ_u²), σ_u²>0. The spread satisfies v_t=φv_{t−1}+η_t with |φ|<1 and iid η_t∼N(0,σ_η²), σ_η²>0. Initialize v₀∼N(0,γ_v), γ_v=σ_η²/(1−φ²), independently of all future spread innovations. The complete spread input (v₀,η₁,η₂,…) is independent of the entire random-walk innovation history. Let y_t=βx_t+v_t, with β≠0. Then y and x share a nonstationary trend, while y_t−βx_t=v_t is stationary: this is cointegration under this model.

The slope is unique among combinations normalized to coefficient one on y. For b≠β, Var(y_t−b x_t)=(β−b)²tσ_u²+γ_v grows with t, so that combination is not covariance stationary. Subtracting adjacent equations gives the exact error-correction representation

Δx_t=u_t,
Δy_t=βΔx_t+(φ−1)(y_{t−1}−βx_{t−1})+η_t.

The adjustment term is part of this same law; it is not a causal interpretation of β. Known-parameter h-step forecasts are βx_t+φ^h v_t, with error variance β²hσ_u²+σ_η²∑_{j=0}^{h−1}φ^{2j}. Independence separates trend and spread forecast errors. Calling y a pure random walk would be inaccurate: its increments include a serially dependent change in the stationary spread.

Conditional slope uncertainty and the T rate. Regress y_t on x_t without an intercept, t=1,…,T, and put D=∑x_t². Conditional on the whole x path, the level-OLS error is centered normal with variance x′Ω_vx/D², where (Ω_v)_{ij}=γ_vφ^{|i−j|}. This uses independence of the entire spread vector from the regressor path, including the stationary initialization. It does not condition on a fixed initial spread or replace Ω_v with γ_vI.

The absolute row sums of Ω_v are at most C_v=γ_v(1+|φ|)/(1−|φ|). The symmetric eigenvalue row bound used earlier implies x′Ω_vx≤C_vD. Meanwhile D/T²⇒σ_u²J by the Brownian-grid Riemann sum, now using right endpoints; its limit is positive. For any δ>0,

P(|T(β̂−β)|>M)≤P(D/T²<δ)+C_v/(δM²).

The second term follows from conditional Chebyshev on D/T²≥δ. Choose δ small enough that the first term is small in the limit, then M large. This proves T(β̂−β)=O_P(1), often called the T rate or superconsistency, and hence ordinary consistency. It does not prove that T(β̂−β) tends to zero, supply an unrestricted normal limit, or justify a usual iid-spread standard error. Estimated residuals also use the fitted β, so their unit-root test law cannot simply be copied from a known observed spread. The inspected MIT cointegration notes motivate this distinction; the restricted construction and rate proof here are explicit.

Worked example 4: the initialization matters for uncertainty

Take β=2, φ=1/2, σ_u²=1, σ_η²=3/4, so γ_v=1. At four recorded dates let x=(1,0,2,3) and v=(1/2,−1/2,1,−1). These are authored illustrative values under a model with stationary random initial spread, not a condition v₀=0. Outcomes are y=(5/2,−1/2,5,5). Since ∑x²=14 and ∑xv=−1/2, the slope is 55/28.

The conditional covariance calculation averages over the stationary spread law given only the x path. It gives x′Ω_vx=87/4 and Var(β̂|x)=87/784. Replacing the spread by iid variance-one errors would give 1/14, which is a different law. From the recorded v values one recovers η₂,η₃,η₄=(−3/4,5/4,−3/2). There is no recorded v₀, so η₁ is not determined.

At the final date, the two-step mean forecast is 2·3+(1/2)²(−1)=23/4. Its error variance is 4·2+(3/4)[1+(1/2)²]=143/16. This forecast conditions on the currently observed spread; that information set differs from conditioning only on the x path in the sampling-variance calculation.

6. Volatility persistence and three different moment questions

Let ε_t=√h_t z_t, with iid z_t, E[z_t]=0, E[z_t²]=1, and

h_t=ω+αε_{t−1}²+βh_{t−1}=ω+A_{t−1}h_{t−1},
A_t=αz_t²+β, ω>0, α≥0, β≥0.

The current h_t is determined by past z and independent of z_t. The one-step conditional law is the scale √h_t times the standardized innovation law. In the finite-variance regime ε_t is a square-integrable martingale difference. Gaussian z makes the one-step conditional law normal; it does not make unconditional returns or a multi-step return sum Gaussian.

A sufficient strict-stationarity construction. Suppose A_t>0 almost surely, E|log A_t|<∞ and E log A_t<0. The integrable iid strong law implies that the log of ∏_{i=1}^j A_{t−i}, divided by j, tends to a negative constant. Its terms are eventually bounded by a geometrically decreasing sequence. Therefore

h_t=ω∑_{j=0}^∞∏_{i=1}^j A_{t−i},

where the empty product is one, is finite almost surely, satisfies the recursion by shifting the sum, and is a strictly stationary causal functional of the iid past. For two finite nonnegative stationary solutions driven by the same multipliers, their difference at t equals the product of m past multipliers times their difference at t−m. The product tends to zero, and the marginal difference is uniformly tight by stationarity of the two solutions. The inequality P(product·|difference|>ε)≤P(product>a)+P(|difference|>ε/a) proves convergence to zero in probability by first taking m large and then a small. Since the difference at t is the same for every m, it must be zero almost surely. This is uniqueness within the stated stationary class, not a general strict-stationarity necessity theorem.

Second moments. Nonnegative-series interchange and independence give E[h_t]=ω∑_{j≥0}(E A)^j. Thus E A=α+β=:ρ<1 gives a finite mean h̄=ω/(1−ρ), and E[ε_t²]=h̄. This also constructs a finite stationary solution directly by finite expectation, even when the separate positive-log hypothesis is not used. If the product-series solution exists but ρ≥1, its expectation is infinite. Strict stationarity and finite return variance are different requirements.

Fourth moments. Suppose κ=E[z⁴]<∞ and define a₂=E[A²]=κα²+2αβ+β². When a₂<1, Cauchy–Schwarz gives ρ≤√a₂<1, and the L² norm of the jth product is a₂^{j/2}. The triangle inequality makes the product series Cauchy in L², so E[h²]<∞. Independence in the squared recursion gives

E[h²]=[ω²+2ωρh̄]/(1−a₂),
E[ε⁴]=κE[h²].

Conversely, if a₂≥1 and a finite E[h²] existed, the same recursion would require (1−a₂)E[h²]=ω²+2ωρE[h]>0, an impossibility. A positive nonnegative h with finite second moment has finite mean, so this contradiction is legitimate. The Gaussian value κ=3 is not distribution free. Raw kurtosis is E[ε⁴]/h̄²; excess kurtosis subtracts 3.

Only after the fourth moment is finite can squared-return covariances be used. Put ν_t=ε_t²−h_t. It is then a square-integrable martingale difference, with variance (κ−1)E[h²] and zero covariance with earlier ν. Substituting h_{t−1}=ε_{t−1}²−ν_{t−1} yields

ε_t²=ω+ρ ε_{t−1}²+ν_t−βν_{t−1}.

This is an ARMA covariance representation of the centered squared process; ν need not be independent or Gaussian. It supports the same linear covariance algebra when its moments exist. If g₀=Var(ε_t²) and g₁=Cov(ε_t²,ε_{t−1}²), then g₁=αg₀+β(E[h²]−h̄²), and g_k=ρ^{k−1}g₁ for k≥1. The first identity follows by conditioning ε_t² on the past; the second follows from the centered recursion and ν orthogonality.

For known parameters and finite conditional variances, the next h is observed through the recursion. Repeated conditioning gives E_t[h_{t+k}]=h̄+ρ^{k−1}(h_{t+1}−h̄), k≥1, when ρ<1. Future return cross moments vanish by the martingale-difference property, so the conditional variance of ∑_{k=1}^H ε_{t+k} is the sum of these H expected variances. This is a variance forecast, not a Gaussian distribution claim. The inspected original Bollerslev paper supplies the historical GARCH and moment context; no QMLE limit or diagnostic-test theorem is inherited.

Worked example 5: persistent variance, and failures of stronger moments

Use ω=1/10, α=1/10, β=4/5 and Gaussian z. Then ρ=9/10 and a₂=83/100. The unconditional return variance is 1, E[h²]=19/17 and E[ε⁴]=57/17. Raw kurtosis is 57/17, so excess kurtosis is 6/17. With h_t=2 and ε_t²=9, h_{t+1}=13/5. The next four variance forecasts are 13/5,61/25,287/125,1354/625; their sum is 5939/625.

The squared-return variance is 40/17. Its lag-one covariance is 28/85 and correlation is 7/50; later correlations decay by powers of 9/10. This squared covariance is well-defined because the fourth moment was established first. At α=0 and β<1 the stationary variance is constant; with Gaussian z the excess kurtosis and squared-return serial covariance are zero.

Change α to 2/5 and β to 1/2, retaining ω=1/10 and Gaussian z. Then ρ=9/10 still gives return variance 1, but a₂=113/100>1, so the return fourth moment is infinite. Squared-return autocovariances no longer have the finite-moment justification just used.

For a different innovation law, let z take values 0,√2,−√2 with probabilities 1/2,1/4,1/4, and use ω=1, α=9/10, β=1/5. Then E[z]=0 and E[z²]=1, while A takes values 1/5 and 2 with equal probabilities. Its expected log is (1/2)log(2/5)≈−0.458145365937, so the positive product series is strictly stationary. Yet E A=11/10>1, and its return variance is infinite. A stationarity claim cannot be substituted for a moment condition.

7. Forecast losses inherit overlap and selection

A forecast comparison must specify the target, loss function, horizon, origin-time information and the procedure producing the forecasts. A fixed known-coefficient forecast, a recursively fitted model and a rule selected after seeing evaluation outcomes have different laws. Historical evaluation also requires the information actually available at each origin, including data vintages; a revised future release is not an original forecast input. The inspected Diebold 2012 working-paper perspective emphasizes these design questions. We do not adopt a normal limit from covariance stationarity alone.

In a random walk with iid N(0,1) increments, the known optimal two-step conditional-mean forecast is x_t. Its error is e_t=u_{t+1}+u_{t+2}. Consecutive errors share one innovation: Var(e_t)=2, Cov(e_t,e_{t+1})=1, and more distant covariances are zero. By the Gaussian fourth-moment identity proved earlier, Cov(e_i²,e_j²)=2Cov(e_i,e_j)². Squared loss is not Gaussian merely because its underlying error is Gaussian.

Compare with the prespecified forecast x_t+c, where c is a fixed number chosen before evaluation. Its squared-loss difference relative to x_t is d_t=(e_t−c)²−e_t²=c²−2ce_t. Thus E[d_t]=c² and the vector of differences is exactly Gaussian. For N consecutive origins,

Var(d̄)=4c²[2N+2(N−1)]/N²,
d̄−c²∼N(0,Var(d̄)).

When c≠0 this supplies an exact standardized normal law with the known covariance sum. At c=0 the loss difference is identically zero; division by a purported positive standard error is inappropriate. The probability statement is for these stipulated fixed forecasts, not for all possible forecast procedures or an unspecified equal-accuracy testing problem.

Choosing c on the evaluation sample changes the experiment. Minimizing c²−2cē gives ĉ=ē and in-sample average difference −ē². On a new block with disjoint future innovations, independent of the entire selection block, expected average difference conditional on ĉ is ĉ². The apparent in-sample improvement therefore has the opposite expected sign from fresh-block performance. An adjacent block that shares an innovation is not the independent block used in this argument.

Worked example 6: exact overlap variance and a selected offset

For N=4, the error covariance matrix has diagonal 2, adjacent off-diagonals 1 and other entries zero. The squared-loss covariance matrix has diagonal 8 and adjacent off-diagonals 2. Average squared loss has mean 2 and variance [4·8+2·3·2]/16=11/4. An iid-row calculation would give only 2.

For the fixed comparison c=1/2, mean loss difference is 1/4. Its average has variance [4·2+2·3·1]/16=7/8, whereas the false iid variance is 1/2. The exact normal statement applies to this linear loss difference; it does not make the average squared loss exactly normal.

If the offset is selected as ē from those four errors, E[ē²]=[4·2+2·3·1]/16=7/8. Expected in-sample difference is −7/8; expected difference on the independent new block is +7/8. With synthetic innovations (1,0,2,−1,1), the four overlapping errors are (1,2,1,0), the selected offset is 1 and its in-sample difference is −1.

Even covariance stationarity alone does not ensure a consistent average or a CLT: let every d_t equal one common centered non-Gaussian random variable Z with finite positive variance. The process is strictly and covariance stationary, but d̄=Z for every N. A HAC label cannot create the missing limit theorem. Estimating loss covariances, reestimating models, selecting among many forecasts or applying nested-model tests requires additional assumptions and proofs beyond the exact finite experiment here.

8. Derive, calculate and audit

  1. Construct the causal L² filter from iid finite-variance innovations and square-summable coefficients, and derive its covariance. Explain why absolute summability also supplies an almost-sure stationary construction. Prove the sufficient inverse-polynomial argument for a repeated factor (1−az)^m, |a|<1, and distinguish causality, invertibility, white noise and conditional-mean forecasting.
  2. Derive the ARMA(1,1) filter, recovery coefficients and h-step mean/error variance. Recompute every mean and variance in example 1. Prove observational equivalence of its two Gaussian MA representations and explain cancellation when θ=−φ.
  3. Prove the VAR covariance-series and Lyapunov uniqueness result under the stated power bound. Recompute example 2's stationary covariance, two-step forecast and both first-shock responses at impact and one period. Explain exactly what the rotation does and does not identify.
  4. For the fixed stable Gaussian AR(1), prove denominator convergence, score orthogonality, the quadratic-form eigenvalue bound, the independent-row smooth-replacement limit and feasible studentization. Calculate the limiting coefficient variance for φ=1/2, σ²=3/4. Why is conditioning on the entire lagged design not the offered proof?
  5. Derive both stated Gaussian unit-root limits from the Brownian-grid law, including positive denominator and residual-variance consistency. Recompute all OLS quantities in the four-increment record in example 3. Identify three changes to the model that would require another limit argument.
  6. Prove cointegration, uniqueness of the normalized slope, the error-correction identity, conditional slope variance and the T rate in the stated independent trend/spread model. Recompute example 4's outcomes, level slope, conditional variance and two-step forecast. Which spread innovations are actually recoverable, and what is conditioned on in each variance statement?
  7. Prove the positive-product sufficient strict-stationarity result and its stated stationary-solution uniqueness. Separately derive the finite return-variance and fourth-moment criteria and formulas. Explain why finite moments must be established before taking squared-return covariances.
  8. For the baseline GARCH case, compute persistence, E[A²], unconditional variance, E[h²], return fourth moment, raw and excess kurtosis, all four conditional variance forecasts and their sum. Derive the squared-process representation, lag-one covariance/correlation and later-lag recurrence.
  9. Analyze both moment-failure transfers in example 5. For the discrete innovation law, verify standardization and the exact expected-log criterion. Contrast strict stationarity, finite return variance and finite fourth moment. What happens to Gaussian excess kurtosis and squared-return serial covariance at α=0, β<1?
  10. Derive the covariance matrices of the four overlapping errors and squared losses in example 6. Derive the exact fixed-c loss-difference law and calculate the correct and false iid variances for c=1/2. Explain the c=0 boundary and give a covariance-stationary counterexample to an automatic averaging CLT.
  11. Derive the evaluation-selected offset and its expected in-sample loss difference. Calculate its expected difference on a genuinely independent new block, and recompute the synthetic selection record. Specify the information/timing condition that an adjacent overlapping block may fail.
  12. A report (i) assigns the stable Gaussian autoregressive score the centered conditional law N(0,σ²D_T) given the entire lagged design; (ii) uses the stable normal slope reference at a unit root; (iii) uses iid standard errors for example 4's serial spread; (iv) rotates a VAR covariance factor and labels its first coordinate a causal policy shock; (v) computes finite squared-return autocovariances for α=2/5, β=1/2 solely because α+β<1; and (vi) selects an offset on its evaluation block and calls the negative fitted loss difference out-of-sample improvement. Give six precise objections, two feasible revised analyses with explicit assumptions, and a defensible conclusion. Use the 12-point solution rubric.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

Reversing the polynomials gives the separate sufficient innovation-recovery condition. (i) The full lagged design fixes all innovations except ε_T; the score is conditionally Gaussian but generally has nonzero conditional mean and variance σ²X_{T−1}², not the claimed centered N(0,σ²D_T) law. The unconditional stable limit needs the supplied quadratic-form argument. (ii) The unit-root denominator grows at a different order and yields a Brownian-functional statistic, so stable normal critical values do not follow. (iii) Stationary AR spread covariance gives 87/784 in the example; replacing it with 1/14 changes the law. (iv) B and BQ generate identical reduced-form Gaussian observations, so a named policy response needs additional identifying restrictions. (v) The specified GARCH transfer has a₂=113/100 and infinite return fourth moment, despite α+β=9/10; the squared covariances lack their moment condition. (vi) Evaluation selection gives expected fitted difference −7/8 but fresh-block difference +7/8; reuse is not out-of-sample performance.

    Two revised analyses, two points each. One defensible revision uses a declared stable or unit-root model and its actual proof-supported normalization, specifies the initialization and regressor information, and keeps causal labels separate from reduced-form forecasts. A second declares the innovation law and moment region, fixes the forecast/tuning procedure before an independent evaluation block, and computes overlap covariance under that actual law. Other revisions earn credit if they name the revised target, justify the relevant assumptions and acknowledge what remains unproved. An arbitrary software standard error or a visual fit is not a substitute.

    Conclusion, two points. The report contains useful model calculations but has not justified the disputed inference, structural labels or performance claim. A corrected study reports which probability law supports each statement, separates fixed-parameter forecasts from estimation and selection uncertainty, and treats empirical suitability as further evidence to establish. The rubric rewards a sound argument rather than a favored model or effect sign.

9. Teach-back and delayed retrieval

Teach-back. Explain why the same least-squares formula has a root-T normal limit in the stable model and a T-scaled Brownian-functional limit at the unit root. Then explain why strictly stationary volatility need not permit a squared-return correlogram.

Answer criteria

In the stable model lagged squares average to a positive constant and the score has a proved root-T normal limit. At the unit root the lagged level accumulates innovations; its squared sum is order T² with a random Brownian-integral limit, while the score is order T and linked to the terminal squared Brownian value. Changing the model changes both normalization and limit law. The GARCH log-product criterion controls pathwise stationarity, the multiplier mean controls finite return variance, and its second moment controls the fourth return moment needed for squared covariances. None of these statements is merely a sample-plot judgment.

Delayed retention. (a) In example 1, what are ψ₁ and the one-step error variance? (b) What is the stable coefficient's root-T limiting variance in example 3? (c) Can η₁ be recovered from example 4's four recorded spreads? (d) What is baseline GARCH excess kurtosis? (e) What happens to the fixed-comparison statistic at c=0?

Retention answers

(a) ψ₁=5/6 and one-step error variance 9/4. (b) 3/4; this is the fixed stable law, not the unit-root law. (c) No: v₀ is not recorded, and stationary initialization is not a value of zero. (d) 6/17; raw kurtosis is 57/17. (e) The difference is identically zero, so a standardized normal statistic with positive denominator is unavailable.

10. Reproduce the calculations without expanding their claims

Run python3 scripts/check_v12_c09.py in the source tree. Successful default execution is quiet. The importable check() returns a strict-JSON-compatible summary and reads only the four canonical payloads. Exact rational filters, matrix/covariance calculations, finite regression identities, product-moment formulas and overlapping-error laws are reconstructed independently. Normal and optimized Python, workspace and exact-four-file isolation, and unrelated working-directory checks are recorded separately from the analytic proofs.

The source specialist inspected selected primary text and thirteen rendered equation pages from five sources: MIT's dated stationarity, VAR and cointegration lectures; Bollerslev's original 1986 paper; and Diebold's September 2012 working paper. The coordinator read the preparation/provenance record and verified retained artifact hashes. The source record preserves the actual body dates, selected pages and explicit cautions. No new full-body or uninspected-appendix reading is claimed. The finite laws and proof organization here are original.

General VAR inference, deterministic-term or non-Gaussian unit-root tests, unrestricted cointegration-rank tests, GARCH QMLE and reestimated or nested forecast-comparison limits require further theory. The next chapter on structural estimation and economic mechanisms connects model parameters to observable restrictions; a reduced-form predictive fit alone does not supply that structural identification. Empirical model assessment and independent human judgment remain separate from these reproducible calculations.

Sources and further study

  • Anna Mikusheva, MIT OpenCourseWare — Lecture Notes 1: Stationarity, Lag Operator, ARMA, and Covariance Structure — Further-study route for covariance stationarity, lag operators and moving-average covariance structure; chapter gives original finite-shock proofs and numerical laws.
  • Lecture Notes 11: VARs — VAR companion/covariance and reduced-form versus structural response distinctions. The chapter independently proves its geometric series and Lyapunov uniqueness without importing the source vec/LR slips or general estimator inference.
  • Lecture Notes 20: Cointegration — Integrated levels with a stationary combination and model-dependent normalizations. The chapter proves a restricted Gaussian Brownian-grid limit and independent stationary-spread T rate, without adopting the source's unproved general functional limits or test laws.
  • Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity — Original GARCH recursion, second/fourth moment distinctions and squared-process covariance context. The positive-log product construction and finite-support infinite-variance transfer are independently derived.
  • Comparing Predictive Accuracy, Twenty Years Later: A Personal Perspective on the Use and Abuse of Diebold-Mariano Tests — Forecast target, serial loss dependence, estimation/selection arrangements and real-time information. The original finite Gaussian overlap/selection proof explicitly rejects stationarity alone as a CLT assumption.
